common_name: Ruby American Persimmon (Named Native Persimmon Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, setting young trees carefully to avoid disturbing the long taproot; like most American persimmon selections, Ruby is dioecious and benefits from a male seedling or another fruiting cultivar planted nearby to help ensure good fruit set.

directions: Ruby is a named selection of the native American persimmon propagated by collectors and specialty nurseries alongside other named cultivars such as Meader, Morris Burton, and Prok. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, its orange fruit remains firm and strongly astringent until fully soft-ripened by cool autumn weather, after which it turns rich, sweet, and custard-like. The species is dioecious, so siting a male tree or another fruiting cultivar nearby helps ensure reliable pollination and fruit set. Established trees tolerate heat, drought, and a wide range of soils, needing little maintenance beyond periodic removal of root suckers to prevent thicket formation.

common_name: Bourgeault Quince (Le Bourgeault, French Heirloom Culinary Quince)

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bourgeault is a vigorous, self-fertile French heirloom quince introduced to North America in the late nineteenth century and needs no second tree for pollination.

directions: Bourgeault, also known as Le Bourgeault, is an old French culinary quince introduced into the United States around 1885 and still propagated today by heirloom fruit specialists. It forms a vigorous, self-fertile tree bearing medium-sized fruit with juicy yellow flesh and good cooking flavor. As with other true quince, the raw fruit is hard and astringent and is not eaten fresh; instead it is prized for jelly, paste, and baked preserves, turning a warm rose color as it cooks down. Grow in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest in fall once the downy skin turns fully golden and gives off the characteristic strong quince fragrance.
sources: Cricket Hill Garden — Cydonia oblonga 'Bourgeault' Heirloom French Quince
Chris Bowers & Sons — Le Bourgeaut Quince Trees

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Isfahan is a traditional Iranian quince selection long grown in the orchards of Isfahan province and studied in Iranian pomological research for its fruit quality.

directions: Isfahan is a long-cultivated traditional quince selection from the orchards of Isfahan province in central Iran, where quince has been grown for centuries alongside other regional culinary fruits. Iranian horticultural researchers have studied it as one of several distinct named quince cultivars grown across the country's fruit-growing regions, valued locally for aromatic, golden fruit used in stews, jams, and preserves. As with other Cydonia oblonga selections, the fruit is hard and astringent when raw and must be cooked to bring out its rich, floral sweetness and characteristic color change. Grow in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest in mid to late fall once the fruit turns fully golden and develops a strong quince fragrance.
